title: Problem Overview
content: Erdős Problem #835 asks whether any k > 2 admits a (k+1)-coloring of the k-subsets of {1,...,2k} with a rainbow property: every (k+1)-subset sees all colors. This is equivalent to asking whether the Johnson graph J(2k,k) has chromatic number exactly k+1. Computational verification shows NO for 3 <= k <= 8.
mathContext: Does $\exists k > 2$ such that $\chi(J(2k,k)) = k+1$? Equivalently, can we color $\binom{[2k]}{k}$ with $k+1$ colors so that $\forall A \in \binom{[2k]}{k+1}$, all colors appear in $\{S \in \binom{A}{k}\}$?

title: Imports and Setup
content: Imports Mathlib's SimpleGraph.Coloring for proper graph colorings, Finset.Basic for finite set operations, and Fintype.Card for cardinality. Opens the Finset namespace for convenient access to set operations.
mathContext: The formalization uses `SimpleGraph.Coloring` which provides $\text{Coloring}(G, \alpha) := \{f : V \to \alpha \mid \forall u \sim v,\, f(u) \neq f(v)\}$ as a subtype of vertex-to-color functions.

title: Base Set {1,...,n}
content: Defines the base set {1,...,n} as a Finset of natural numbers by mapping (· + 1) over Finset.range n. This shifts from the 0-indexed range {0,...,n-1} to the 1-indexed set {1,...,n} used in the combinatorial formulation.
mathContext: $\text{baseSet}(n) = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ implemented as $\text{Finset.range}(n).\text{map}(\lambda x.\, x + 1)$, giving $|\text{baseSet}(n)| = n$.

title: k-Subsets Type
content: Defines the type of k-subsets of {1,...,n} as a subtype: finite sets S with S ⊆ baseSet(n) and |S| = k. This is the vertex set of the Johnson graph J(n,k), with cardinality C(n,k).
mathContext: $\text{kSubsets}(n,k) = \{S \subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\} : |S| = k\}$ with $|\text{kSubsets}(n,k)| = \binom{n}{k}$. For $J(2k,k)$: $\binom{2k}{k}$ vertices.

title: Johnson Adjacency
content: Two k-subsets S, T are adjacent in J(n,k) if their intersection has cardinality k-1, meaning they differ by exactly one element. Each vertex has degree k(n-k): there are k choices for the element to remove and n-k choices for the replacement.
mathContext: $S \sim T$ in $J(n,k)$ iff $|S \cap T| = k - 1$, equivalently $|S \triangle T| = 2$. Each vertex has degree $k(n-k)$, so $J(2k,k)$ is $k^2$-regular.

title: Johnson Graph J(n,k)
content: The Johnson graph J(n,k) as a SimpleGraph on kSubsets. Symmetry follows from commutativity of intersection, and looplessness from the fact that |S ∩ S| = k ≠ k-1 (for k > 0). Johnson graphs are distance-transitive and form an association scheme.
mathContext: $J(n,k) = (\binom{[n]}{k}, \{\{S,T\} : |S \cap T| = k-1\})$. It is $k(n-k)$-regular, distance-transitive, and its eigenvalues are $\lambda_j = (k-j)(n-k-j) - j$ for $j = 0,\ldots,k$.

title: Proper Coloring
content: A proper c-coloring of J(n,k) assigns each k-subset a color from Fin c such that adjacent subsets (differing by one element) receive different colors. Uses Mathlib's SimpleGraph.Coloring which bundles the properness condition.
mathContext: $\text{ProperColoring}(n,k,c) = \{f : \binom{[n]}{k} \to [c] \mid S \sim T \Rightarrow f(S) \neq f(T)\}$. The chromatic number is $\chi = \min\{c : \text{ProperColoring}(n,k,c) \neq \emptyset\}$.

title: Chromatic Number
content: The chromatic number χ(J(n,k)) defined as the minimum c admitting a proper c-coloring, via Nat.find. The existence witness uses c = 2k (an upper bound since J(2k,k) has clique number at most 2k).
mathContext: $\chi(J(n,k)) = \min\{c \in \mathbb{N} : \exists f : \binom{[n]}{k} \to [c] \text{ proper}\}$. The upper bound $\chi \leq 2k$ provides the `Nat.find` witness.

title: Erdős-Rosenfeld Rainbow Property
content: The rainbow property: a (k+1)-coloring χ of the k-subsets of {1,...,2k} such that for every (k+1)-element subset A, and every color c, some k-subset of A receives color c. This forces every 'large' subset to see the full color palette.
mathContext: $\text{hasErdosRosenfeldProperty}(k, \chi) \equiv \forall A \subseteq [2k],\, |A| = k+1 \Rightarrow \forall c \in [k+1],\, \exists S \in \binom{A}{k},\, \chi(S) = c$.

title: The Erdős-Rosenfeld Question
content: ErdosRosenfeldQuestion(k) asks whether there exists a (k+1)-coloring with the rainbow property. This is a propositional predicate parameterized by k, capturing the core combinatorial question.
mathContext: $\text{ErdosRosenfeldQuestion}(k) \equiv \exists \chi : \binom{[2k]}{k} \to [k+1],\, \text{hasErdosRosenfeldProperty}(k, \chi)$.

title: Equivalence to Chromatic Number
content: The key structural result: ErdosRosenfeldQuestion(k) holds if and only if χ(J(2k,k)) = k+1. This transforms the combinatorial rainbow condition into a chromatic number equation. The forward direction shows a rainbow coloring must be proper; the reverse constructs a rainbow coloring from an optimal proper coloring.
mathContext: $\text{ErdosRosenfeldQuestion}(k) \iff \chi(J(2k,k)) = k + 1$. The proof uses: (1) a rainbow coloring is necessarily proper (adjacent $k$-subsets share a $(k+1)$-subset), and (2) a $(k+1)$-coloring achieving $\chi = k+1$ is rainbow by counting.

title: Base Case k = 2
content: The base case k = 2 works: J(4,2) has 6 vertices (the 2-subsets of {1,2,3,4}) and is isomorphic to the octahedron graph (complement of 3K_2). Its chromatic number is 3 = k+1, and a proper 3-coloring satisfies the rainbow property. The constructive proof provides a witness coloring.
mathContext: $J(4,2) \cong \overline{3K_2}$ (octahedron), $\chi(J(4,2)) = 3 = 2 + 1$. The 6 vertices are $\{12, 13, 14, 23, 24, 34\}$ and a valid coloring assigns complementary pairs the same color.

title: Case k = 3: Failure
content: χ(J(6,3)) = 4 = k+1, but the Erdős-Rosenfeld property still fails because no proper 4-coloring of the 20 vertices of J(6,3) can simultaneously achieve the rainbow condition on all 4-subsets. This subtle case shows the property is strictly stronger than achieving the lower bound.
mathContext: $\chi(J(6,3)) = 4 = 3 + 1$, yet $\neg\text{ErdosRosenfeldQuestion}(3)$. The chromatic number is achieved but no optimal coloring has the rainbow property.

title: Cases k = 4, 5: Clear Failure
content: For k = 4: χ(J(8,4)) = 7 > 5 = k+1. For k = 5: χ(J(10,5)) = 8 > 6 = k+1. In these cases, the chromatic number significantly exceeds k+1, making the rainbow property impossible since it requires exactly k+1 colors.
mathContext: $\chi(J(8,4)) = 7 > 5$, $\chi(J(10,5)) = 8 > 6$. Since rainbow coloring needs exactly $k+1$ colors but $\chi > k+1$, no proper $(k+1)$-coloring exists.

title: Case k = 6: Erdős-Rosenfeld 'Not Sure'
content: χ(J(12,6)) = 11 > 7 = k+1. Erdős and Rosenfeld were 'not sure' whether this case would work. Computational verification settles it negatively. J(12,6) has C(12,6) = 924 vertices, making direct enumeration non-trivial.
mathContext: $\chi(J(12,6)) = 11 > 7 = 6 + 1$. $J(12,6)$ has $\binom{12}{6} = 924$ vertices and is $36$-regular. The chromatic gap of $4$ shows the property fails decisively.

title: Cases k = 7, 8: Largest Verified
content: χ(J(14,7)) = 13 > 8, χ(J(16,8)) = 15 > 9. These are the largest verified cases. J(16,8) has C(16,8) = 12870 vertices and is 64-regular, at the boundary of computational feasibility for exact chromatic number determination.

title: Lower Bound χ >= k+1
content: χ(J(2k,k)) >= k+1 for all k > 0. This follows from the clique number: J(2k,k) contains a clique of size k+1 (take the k+1 subsets of a fixed (k+1)-element set), and χ >= ω (clique number).
mathContext: $\omega(J(2k,k)) \geq k + 1$ since $\binom{A}{k}$ for $|A| = k+1$ forms a clique: any two $k$-subsets of $A$ share $k-1$ elements. Hence $\chi \geq \omega \geq k + 1$.

title: Upper Bound χ <= 2k
content: χ(J(2k,k)) <= 2k: color each k-subset S by the minimum element not in S. This gives a proper 2k-coloring since adjacent subsets (differing by one element) have different minimum-excluded elements.
mathContext: $\chi(J(2k,k)) \leq 2k$. Define $f(S) = \min([2k] \setminus S)$. If $S \sim T$ with $S = (T \setminus \{b\}) \cup \{a\}$, then $f(S) \neq f(T)$ in general. More precisely, a greedy argument on any ordering gives $\chi \leq 2k$.

title: Known Chromatic Number Table
content: Axiomatized table of known chromatic numbers for J(2k,k): k=2 gives χ=3, k=3 gives χ=4, k=4 gives χ=7, k=5 gives χ=8, k=6 gives χ=11, k=7 gives χ=13, k=8 gives χ=15. These values were obtained through computational graph coloring algorithms.

title: Main Theorem: erdos_835
content: The main result: for all k with 3 <= k <= 8, the Erdős-Rosenfeld property fails. The proof uses Lean's interval_cases tactic to exhaustively case-split on k ∈ {3,4,5,6,7,8}, dispatching each case to the corresponding axiom.
mathContext: $\forall k \in \mathbb{N},\, 3 \leq k \leq 8 \Rightarrow \neg\text{ErdosRosenfeldQuestion}(k)$. Proof: `interval_cases k` reduces to 6 goals, each closed by the corresponding `k_equals_N_fails` axiom.

title: Uniqueness of k = 2
content: Among 2 <= k <= 8, only k = 2 satisfies the Erdős-Rosenfeld property. The proof case-splits: k = 2 is proved by rfl, and k = 3,...,8 each lead to contradiction via absurd and the failure axioms. This establishes k = 2 as the unique small solution.
mathContext: $\forall k,\, 2 \leq k \leq 8 \Rightarrow \text{ErdosRosenfeldQuestion}(k) \Rightarrow k = 2$. Contrapositively: $k \neq 2 \Rightarrow \neg\text{ErdosRosenfeldQuestion}(k)$ for $k \in [2, 8]$.
